        Protests escalated in France over the weekend over living costs and education, raising concerns over the NFL game between the Pittsburgh Steelers and New Orleans Saints scheduled to take place in Paris next week. The unrest stems in part from citizens demanding better school conditions, teacher shortages and public services, but it has since grown as violent groups have rioted, clashed with police, and set fire to public buildings. At least 1,800 across the country, according to CBS News. Hundreds of thousands have taken to the streets across the nation to demand change from the government, as both protesters and law enforcement have turned to violent methods. Concern over player, personnel, and fan safety has become the main topic surrounding next week's international game, the first-ever regular-season matchup to take place in France.The league released a statement last week saying they still plan to conduct the game as scheduled on Oct. 25 and provided a similar update on Sunday after news of the social unrest spread."Preparations continue as scheduled for NFL events and the game at Stade de France next Sunday," the NFL said. "We continue to work closely with local authorities and partners on all operational and security matters. We are also providing the two clubs with regular updates. There's been no disruption or impact at league sites."
Saints executive Greg Bensel backed the league's statement and offered some insight into the league's safety precautions. "We concur with the NFL's statement and are planning to play the game. In addition to working closely with the NFL, we have also maintained daily security updates with our security partners in France," Bensel said. "Members of our football operations staff and internal security team have been on the ground in France for the past few days and there has been no disruption or impact at any of our team sites."Last week, the league's statement said, "We're excited for the first-ever regular season game in Paris, and preparations continue as scheduled for NFL events and the game at Stade de France on October 25. As we do for every NFL game, including our international games, we work closely with local authorities and partners on all operational and security matters. We look forward to welcoming fans to Paris later this month."
The game is scheduled for 9:30 a.m. ET, 2:30 p.m. local time. The Saints are scheduled to leave Sunday night and spend the week practicing in France.The league has changed games in the past due to various factors, including weather and field conditions, so it is not entirely out of the realm of possibility that the game could be moved. The Saints are considered the home team, so if they did move it, which they clearly do not plan to do right now, New Orleans would be the obvious new location.While protests have taken over Paris, it's not the only place in France affected. Here's more from CBS News:
"Authorities said masked groups on Saturday set fires and attacked public buildings, including city halls, in several cities."In Limoges, a city in central France, flames engulfed the 19th-century City Hall, causing its roof to collapse. Haute-Vienne prefect Maurice Barate told LCI television that the fire was deliberately set and nearly destroyed the building. The fire was under control Sunday.""Around Paris' Place de la République on Sunday morning, dislodged cobblestones, shattered storefronts and broken glass marked the aftermath of the events. Looting and damage were reported around the square and in some other tourist and shopping areas in the city center."Paris police said Sunday that 855 people were arrested in the French capital region alone. The Paris prosecutors' office said that 557 of them were kept in police custody."

In the aftermath of SummerSlam, Oba Femi and the weekend's other big winners are ready to forge ahead. WWE historically has four cornerstone events. Three have been crossed off this year's calendar: Royal Rumble, WrestleMania and SummerSlam. More recently, the "Big Four" has expanded to the "Big Five," and dates are set for the two remaining marquee events.  First is the youngest of the five pillar shows. WWE heads to New Orleans for Money in the Bank with its titular multi-person ladder matches. The winners of the men's and  women's Money in the Bank earn title shots at a time and place of their  choosing. That unique advantage has translated to an 82% success rate for  the briefcase holders.   
Completing the quintet is Survivor Series, which takes place in Houston on Nov. 28. The event traditionally features eponymous multi-man elimination tag team matches. Since 2022, those matches have been replaced by WarGames. The legendary WarGames match, created by Dusty Rhodes in the '80s, takes place inside an enormous steel cage housing two rings. Two teams battle with participants entering individually at timed intervals. Only once all competitors are in the ring can the match be won by pinfall or submission. Sandwiched between them is Crown Jewel, which returns to Saudi Arabia on Nov. 7.         Wide receiver Marvin Harrison Jr. has made the first of likely many catches as a member of the Houston Texans. Harrison's Texans debut comes across the pond, at Wembley Stadium in England against the Jacksonville Jaguars on Sunday.Harrison's reunion with his former Ohio State quarterback C.J. Stroud was highly anticipated following the wide receiver's trade from the Arizona Cardinals last week. The former No. 4 overall pick got his first action in the second quarter, catching a 14-yard pass from Stroud.
He made another catch, this time for 15 yards, in the third quarter, with the Texans up 17-14. The 24-year-old now has three receptions on four targets for 34 yards. 
Stroud had nothing but good things to say about his newest teammate as the trade rumors were swirling earlier this month. He called Harrison an "amazing talent," "great teammate," and "one of the hardest workers" he's ever known. Harrison was inactive for last week's game, his final as a member of the Cardinals. With Arizona, he didn't live up to the hype he had going into the league. 
Through 33 games, going into this week, Harrison has 108 receptions, 1,578 receiving yards and 13 touchdowns.

        Coming into Week 6, we knew things were going to be rough. This is one of the toughest bye weeks of the season, with five of the top 20 players on Draft Day off. The injury situation isn't making things any easier. There is positive news around Caleb Williams' return and even better news on A.J. Brown. Both are expected to play and they will be ranked as starters. Most of the other news this week has not been good. Nowhere has the news been as bad as it has been in Philadelphia.Update: Henderson 'good to go'TreVeyon Henderson is 'good to go' according to NFL Network's Mike Garafolo and will be mixed in with the Patriots' backs in Week 6. He is someone best left on your bench as he has lost key red zone and passing down snaps to Rhamondre Stevenson of late.A.J. Brown is ready to rockBrown is back for the Patriots and apparently had an excellent week of practice without any limitations. He's expected to have a full workload in Week 6 and should be in all starting lineups. Jalen Hurts and Saquon Barkley out, DeVonta Smith is backThe long-term prognosis is still very much in the air, but what we do know is that Hurts won't play Week 6 against the Carolina Panthers. In his place will be Tanner McKee, who will play behind a makeshift line, possibly without Barkley, who was also ruled out. Smith was removed from the injury report and will make his return, but because of the absence of Hurts, he'll rank as a borderline WR2. The Eagles' implied total has fallen to 17.75, one of the lowest marks of the week. McKee has made two starts in his NFL career and thrown 88 career passes. Both of his starts were in Week 18, so it is hard to know what, if anything, to take from them. We mostly agree with the line movement that this is a significant downgrade. Dameon Pierce will replace Barkley and he projects as a low-end RB2 only because the position is so thin this week. Dontayvion Wicks and Makai Lemon fall to desperation flex range with Smith back.
Quinshon Judkins limited, KC Concepcion clears concussion protocolJudkins was in a walking boot on Sunday, and his backup, Raheim Sanders, was placed on Injured Reserve earlier in the week. That leaves Jaleel McLaughlin and Audric Estime, who the team just signed. McLaughlin would be a mediocre flex if Judkins is out. Judkins would be a high-end flex if he plays. With Concepcion cleared, view him as a flex and Boston as a boom/bust WR3.TreVeyon Henderson questionableHenderson has a high ankle sprain, so we didn't think he had any chance to play. The fact that he practiced this week suggests otherwise. Rhamondre Stevenson will be ranked as a top 18 back either way, but he is a borderline top 12 option if Henderson is out. Henderson hasn't been startable for most of the season and we won't want to start him if he plays through the ankle injury.Lamar Jackson ruled outThis is another downgrade to the passing game, but we are still starting Zay Flowers as a WR2. Mark Andrews should be left on your bench with Tyler Huntley starting. Ja'Kobi Lane is trying to get back from his IR stint and practiced in full this week. We don't have him ranked yet, but would love to see him back. Rashod Bateman was a limited participant on Wednesday, did not practice on Thursday and was back in a limited capacity on Friday. Neither of these guys will be ranked as more than a desperation flex if they play, but Lane may be someone worth stashing in deeper leagues. 
Tyjae Spears returns on FridaySpears was a limited participant on Wednesday, sat out Thursday with a knee issue, and logged a full practice on Friday. We are expecting Spears to be active as the 1B back behind Tony Pollard. Pollard is a low-end RB2 this week and Spears is a low-end PPR flex. Rico Dowdle logs full practice on Thursday and FridayWe are moving Dowdle into our rankings even though he was listed as questionable on the final injury report. This was close to an even split the first two weeks of the season but the Steelers have acknowledged that Jaylen Warren has been way too good to go back to an even timeshare. I am projecting 17 touches for Warren and 9 for Dowdle. That means Warren is still a top 12 running back while Dowdle is a decent flex. Rashee Rice ruled outRice suffered a hamstring injury in Week 4 and the bye week was not enough to get him back to 100%. The Chiefs are already without Tyquan Thornton, so Patrick Mahomes will need Jalen Royals and Cyrus Allen to play a major role against the Chargers. Xavier Worthy is an upside WR3 and both Royals and Allen are deep flexes. Mahomes falls just outside of the top 12, and I would rather start Kirk Cousins.
Kyle Monangai also outIt will be another week of D'Andre Swift and Roschon Johnson at running back for the Bears. Swift is an RB1 that should be started in all leagues, while Johnson is more of a low-end flex. They rotated drives last week, but Johnson was extremely inefficient as a rusher. If Monangai returns on Friday, he could be a high-end flex in Week 6.Jacory Croskey-Merrit not practicing FridayCroskey-Merritt has not missed two practices for the Commanders, who play San Francisco on Monday. This backfield is a mess right now with Croskey-Merritt, Rachaad White, and Austin Ekeler all getting touches and all on the injury report. I don't really want to start any of them, especially against a good defense like the 49ers. That being said, Croskey-Merritt is our favorite if he plays. If he's out, then Rachaad White becomes much more appealing as a high-end flex, especially in PPR.Ladd McConkey and Quentin Johnston are off the injury reportJustin Herbert is finally getting some help. We still don't want to start him, but we do view McConkey as a WR3 with top 12 upside if he is truly 100%. Johnston is more of a boom/bust flex; he has had a very difficult time getting going. The Chargers' offensive line is still a massive problem and their implied total of 16.75 doesn't offer much reason for optimism.
Jeremiyah Love still not practicingLove has an ankle injury, but he also sounds really run-down. The Cardinals are giving him the week off, which makes Tyler Allgeier is a high-end flex, right around RB25 in the rankings.. This is a bad matchup and the Cardinals will probably be chasing the score, so Allgeier will need work in the passing game to produce a good Fantasy day.David Montgomery not traveling to LondonWoody Marks will be the lead back for the Texans in an uneven matchup. The Jaguars are arguably the best run defense in football, but they are also giving up six catches per week to opposing running backs. It's a statement on this week's position that Marks is a top-20 back because we are very concerned about his rushing efficiency, but he should catch enough passes to be startable in PPR.Tyler Warren suffered groin injury at Friday's practiceWarren is listed as questionable, but we never like it when a guy picks up a new injury this late in the week. Be prepared to replace Warren if he is your only tight end. If he does miss Week 6, that would be a boost in targets for Josh Downs and Keenan Allen. Downs would be a borderline WR2 without Warren and Allen would be a solid WR3.

title: NFL addresses safety concerns for Steelers-Saints game in France protests in Paris continues - CBS Sports
description: The league says it is still planning to play the game as originally scheduled
body:
The league says it is still planning to play the game as originally scheduled

    12:34 pm ET

        With protests on their third week in Paris and an NFL game scheduled to take place in the city in just a week, growing concern over fan and player safety has left some wondering if the league will alter any of its plans. But the NFL said on Wednesday that the game will go on as scheduled, with the Pittsburgh Steelers and New Orleans Saints meeting on Oct. 25 at the Stade de France in Saint-Denis, located just north of Paris."We're excited for the first-ever regular season game in Paris, and preparations continue as scheduled for NFL events and the game at Stade de France on October 25," the NFL said in a statement earlier this week, via ESPN. "As we do for every NFL game, including our international games, we work closely with local authorities and partners on all operational and security matters. We look forward to welcoming fans to Paris later this month."As protests continue, the league released another statement emphasizing that they plan to play the game in Paris."Preparations continue as scheduled for NFL events and the game at Stade de France next Sunday," the NFL said. "We continue to work closely with local authorities and partners on all operational and security matters. We are also providing the two clubs with regular updates. There's been no disruption or impact at league sites."
The social unrest stems from demands for the government to change multiple aspects of the education system. Protestors are asking the government to address under-resourced schools, poor conditions and teacher shortages. Students say the schools are falling apart and rats are in the buildings. The protests have sparked violence, with authorities using tear gas, stun grenades and various other means to attempt to stop the crowds. Protestors have reportedly set fires and caused damage. Police detained over 5,000 people in connection with protests, according to CBS News. Local officials say they are investigating both the protests and the police response. 
The French government is currently in a "political deadlock" as they approach the presidential elections in the spring. They have not responded to protestors with any plans or solutions for their complaints and demands. If the situation in Paris escalates, the NFL could reconsider its stance, but right now, it is sticking with its original plan. The NFL has changed game locations in the past due to extreme weather or field conditions. The Saints are considered the home team for the game, and their only listed event for the day in New Orleans is a private event where youth and amateur sports teams have the chance to play inside the stadium. It is scheduled for 8:30 a.m. local time, so if needed, the game could seemingly be played at Caesar's Superdome. But that seems unlikely at the moment.
If the game does go on as planned, it will mark the first-ever NFL game played in France.  This will be the second straight year the Steelers play a game outside the United States, having played in Dublin last season against the Minnesota Vikings. The Saints last played an international game in 2022, visiting London to face the Vikings.

title: Tom Fornelli's CFP Vibe Check: No matter how big playoff field gets, no game will ever be meaningless - CBS Sports
description: Every week the CFP Vibe Check tries to put its finger on where things stand in the College Football Playoff race without overreacting to
body:
Every week the CFP Vibe Check tries to put its finger on where things stand in the College Football Playoff race without overreacting to what it just saw, but also probably overreacting to everything it just saw. There may not have been a better weekend of college football to reflect the week's news in the sport. If you had your head in the sand all week, the College Football Playoff is expanding to 24 teams. The news came and was not well-met by most of the college football literati, or the more vocal sect of college football fans online.But Saturday might have caused some to reconsider.To be clear, I am not a proponent of expanding the field to 24. In fact, I spent years arguing against expanding to 12, and for many of the same reasons you hear people arguing against expanding to 24. But when I stopped yelling and looked around at the current state of the sport, I realized 12 made sense. Maybe 16 would make even more.We're never going to see NFL-style parity in college football, but we're seeing far more of it than ever before. It's been brought on by a host of different changes. Conference realignment is the primary factor. It has concentrated so many of the sport's traditional powers into a few conferences and forced them to play each other all the time when, in eras of yore, those same teams might meet once per decade, if at all. Toss in NIL and a transfer portal, and suddenly the talent becomes a little more evenly distributed at the top.
When all that happens, a bunch of strange things occur. Whether it's Indiana winning a national title, or eight top-20 teams -- and five of the top-10 -- losing in the same weekend. That's what happened this week, and things were almost more chaotic than that.Miami needed double-overtime to beat Florida State. Had the Hurricanes lost, it would've been the first time in the history of the AP Top 25 -- which began in 1936 -- that the top three teams in the poll all lost during the same week.These are the kinds of results that just didn't happen through the sports history. They're the kinds of results that are far more likely to happen in a 24-team playoff than they would've been if the 24-team playoff existed a decade ago before the portal and NIL. 
It's possible to both long for a time when every loss was a deathblow while also realizing holding teams to that same standard in this era just isn't fair anymore. You can find all sorts of people to blame for what's happened, but it doesn't change the fact that everybody is still watching, and we're all still feeling every single emotion.
Seriously, I got a bit teary-eyed on Saturday. After spending a good portion of the week hearing and reading angry thoughts about how the sport was dying, on Saturday I saw the complete opposite. I saw Auburn coach Alex Golesh fighting back tears, one arm around his son, while giving a postgame interview after Auburn's first win over Georgia in Athens since 2005. I saw Tennessee fans storming the field at Neyland Stadium and lighting up cigars. I saw North Carolina players sprinting to the Victory Bell to reclaim it after beating Duke. I saw BYU fans storm the field after one of the biggest wins in program history.I saw the other side, too. I saw Texas fans in disbelief that they'd lost to Florida again. I saw a broken-hearted Nick Marsh wishing he could disappear from the face of the Earth after realizing what he thought was his game-winning touchdown catch was an incompletion because he stepped out of bounds. 
I saw all of it and knew that, no matter how big the playoff field gets, no college football game will ever be meaningless. No matter how many angry tweets or social media clips you see.Anybody who doesn't see that does so because they choose to.The Big 12 emerged from the chaos in a great spotBYU's thrilling 28-24 win over Notre Dame wasn't just a huge moment for the program, but a great win for a Big 12 conference that has never received much credit from the College Football Playoff selection committee. It was the kind of marquee win the conference had lacked out of conference since 2024's new orer. 
It was also the first step in the scenario I wrote about last week: the Big 12 not just getting two teams in, but three. Now, as I wrote last week, it's a bit far-fetched, but after the carnage of Week 7, it's a lot more likely. BYU wasn't the only Big 12 program to win this week. Both Texas Tech and Utah held serve to remain undefeated, and Houston picked up a win against Oklahoma State.
BYU now has the best odds in the conference at DraftKings, going from +200 (33.3%) to -140 (58.3%) after the win over the Irish. Texas Tech went from +120 (45.5%) to -110 (52.8%). Houston went from +800 (11.1%) to +475 (17.4%). Oddly, Utah's odds fell from +105 to +115. Still, if you add up the implied odds of every Big 12 team currently listed at DraftKings, the Big 12 is currently at 1.94 teams.It's a much better position than they were at the beginning of the season.The other side of thingsNotre Dame's margin of error got a lot thinner Saturday night. The Irish entered the weekend with the best odds in the country of making the playoff. The good news is they still have the third-best odds.The bad news is the odds aren't nearly as good. The Irish went from -4000 (97.6%) to -1000 (90.9%). It's a pretty significant drop, and clearly most people expected Notre Dame to beat BYU. Now the team with the best odds in the country is the toughest test remaining on Notre Dame's schedule: Miami.
If there's a silver lining, it's that while the Irish were part of the wreckage on Saturday, they did benefit from it a little. If everything else around the country had gone according to plan, the Irish would be looking at a situation where if they lost to Miami, they were very likely to miss the playoffs for the same reason they missed last year: a good record, but no marquee win.Now there's more of an argument for a 10-2 Notre Dame even if it loses to Miami simply because there may not be many other 10-2 teams out there. I can't help but wonder where Notre Dame's odds would be if not for all the other upsets this weekend. I'm guessing they'd be far closer to Alabama (-250) or even BYU than Georgia (-1100) and Miami (-2500).Oh, and that's one other thing worth mentioning. Miami has the best odds right now at -2500. That same number would've been good for third-best before the weekend. 
The field has opened up a bit for everybody.It's anybody's guess in the SECThere are two ways to look at what happened in the SEC on Saturday. One is that five of the league's top 20 teams lost. The other is that the SEC picked up five wins over top-20 teams on Saturday!However you want to look at it, what's left is a pretty jumbled mess, and I'm not sure how it impacts the league's ability to dominate the field at the end of the year. The one thing I am pretty confident in at this point is that we will have a 9-3 team in the field this year, and it may be because the SEC champion finishes the regular season at 9-3.What should be a serious cause of concern for the league is that it's gone from having a great chance of getting five into the field to looking at four at best. While Georgia has the second-best odds, the next best team is Alabama at -250 (71.4%). Ole Miss -125 (55.6%) is eighth, and Texas +110 (47.6%) is tenth. 
Texas, thanks to its 27-24 loss to Florida, is now behind both BYU and Texas Tech on the odds board. I'm sure that won't be brought up in conversations across the Lone Star State this week.What might be stranger to comprehend is that both LSU and Tennessee are at +154 (39.4%), which puts them behind UCLA and Boise State. Kentucky is behind James Madison. Missouri and Mississippi State fell so far down the board that the oddsmakers are basically saying they don't believe either has a chance, but maybe somebody will be dumb enough to bet on them.The SEC is the only Power Four conference that doesn't have any undefeated teams remaining in conference play, and most teams aren't even halfway through their SEC slate. There's going to be a lot more chaos in this league before all is said and done.
Beware of Ohio State
The Buckeyes scored a huge win over Indiana on Saturday, but it came at a considerable cost. Julian Sayin finished the game on the sideline with his throwing arm in a sling, and Ryan Day said after the game that Ohio State's starting quarterback will miss "several weeks."There's a lot of leeway in that assessment, and the Buckeyes are on a bye next week. So depending on the severity of the injury and Ryan Day's definition of "several," it's possible Sayin might not miss a game.I think it's more likely he misses at least one, and Ohio State's next game is at USC on Halloween. The following week it's Oregon in Columbus. While he was thrown into one hell of a fire, backup Luke Fahey did not inspire much confidence after replacing Sayin.
So I was quite surprised to see Ohio State's odds of reaching the playoff improve from -750 (88.2%) to -950 (90.5%). On the other side of the game, Indiana went from -800 (88.8%) to -700 (87.5%), and I'm more confident in the Hoosiers right now than the Buckeyes. They're healthier and have an easier finish to their schedule.My rooting interest
Listen, I'm not supposed to root for teams in this job. I get that. But I'm also human, and I'd be lying to you if I didn't say I want Oregon State to be the Group of Six representative in this year's playoff.They're not currently the favorite. In fact, they're currently behind Boise State, James Madison, New Mexico and UTSA with odds of +1200 (7.7%). All those teams should have better odds, and I mean no disrespect to them.But I'd rather watch Oregon State. Honestly, they feel like the most dangerous G6 team, at least, in a playoff sense. If you haven't seen what this Beavers offense has done all year, I recommend checking them out. The QB/WR combination of Braden Atkinson and Jesse LeGree has been something to behold.Perhaps you saw some of it earlier in the season when the Beavers lost at Houston 33-20, or at home to Texas Tech 35-24. Seriously, Oregon State gave both of them more problems than a few of the Big 12 teams they've faced have.Whoever earns the spot earns the spot, but just know I'll be hoping it's Oregon State that does so from this point forward.Week 8 Vibe ShiftersA look ahead to the five games on next week's slate most likely to impact the playoff raceOle Miss at TexasHouston at UtahIndiana at MichiganLSU at AuburnNorth Dakota State at New MexicoThis week's CFP projectionAs if anybody knows after the weekend we just had.MiamiGeorgiaIndianaBYUOhio StateAlabamaNotre DameOle MissTexas TechUCLALSUBoise State

title: Why Kevin Durant completely missed Mat Ishbia's point about championship culture - CBS Sports
description: It's easy to see how Durant would take offense to Ishbia's comments, but there was a bit more context to what the
body:
It's easy to see how Durant would take offense to Ishbia's comments, but there was a bit more context to what the Suns owner was saying
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 18, 2026
                            
                    at
    10:26 am ET
                        
                •
            
            7 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        Kevin Durant is playing the "blame KD" hashtag card on social media after Suns owner Mat Ishbia went on CNBC and said, "bringing in super talented players like Kevin Durant doesn't necessarily lead to championships." There was a bit more context to Ishbia's comments, which we'll get to, but Durant took offense to the headline and, predictably, fired back at Ishbia. And so ensued the following exchange: Durant: #blameKD even though KD stayed on top of his game at 36 and got u back this "culture" you love so much. Aye, Matthew acts like I got arrested for a DUI or sumn. Back to threads 😂😂😂😂😂😂😂Ishbia: You obviously didn't watch the clip. 😂 Didn't blame you @Kdtrey5, but am happy with the culture we are building here in Phoenix. We got the right guys and right focus now and are excited for this season. ... Good luck this season in Houston.Durant: U should be giving Thanks every chance u get. You don't have to pay me an absurd amount of money to play for another team.So let's address this one comment at a time, beginning with Ishbia's original answer, in its entirety, when he was asked on CNBC what, with the benefit of hindsight, he had learned from the trade his Suns made for Durant two days after his purchase of the team became official in February of 2023. Ishbia's full comments"The team was I think the [No.] 8 or 9 seed [in the Western Conference] when I bought the team," Ishbia said. "We had some good young players, and [the question was]: Can we get over the top? I basically was told, 'Hey, as an owner, stay out of it. Give them some money. And so I said, 'Hey listen, we'll go into the luxury tax, go do whatever it takes to try to win a championship."And so, we did that," Ishbia continued. "But it was more going and getting Kevin Durant. Which ... good player, done a lot of great things, won two championships before, but it was not aligned with my vision. We had a couple years and it did not succeed, as we're well aware of at this point."After that year, I decided [to] trade Kevin Durant, bring in my [own] GM (Brian Gregory replaced James Jones), bring in a new coach (Jordan Ott replaced Mike Budenholzer, who had replaced Frank Vogel), and get extremely involved personally with the type of guy and type of person we want in the organization, not just on the court but off the court."I'm not saying [that type of person is] Kevin Durant or not Kevin Durant, but here's what I will say: It is Dillon Brooks. It is Jordan Goodwin. It is Collin Gillespie. Of course Devin Booker. I'm not going to name every one of my players, but we've defined what matters to us. We have a thing called Suns DNA. The type of player that we believe in, that we want, and it's a team that the fans will be proud of. "Everyone thought we were going to be the worst team in the league last year. We made the playoffs. Won 45 games. We're going to build on that. So what I've learned, my biggest lesson ... it's not positive or negative about Kevin Durant. We have to define what we're about in Phoenix, and then stick with it. And believe in our vision and our path. And I didn't do that in the beginning. I kind of just threw money at the problem.
"... There was not a defined culture and North Star where we were going [as an organization]," Ishbia concluded. "And therefore, bringing in super-talented players like Kevin Durant doesn't necessarily lead to championships."Does Ishbia have a point?Of course he does. In fact, he didn't even really need the "necessarily" qualification. Unless we're talking about the Warriors (who had Stephen Curry, and, by extension, the sort of foundational championship culture to which Ishbia is referring, and were therefore an exception to this rule), bringing in Durant has definitively not led to championships -- or frankly even honest championship contention. Not for the Nets. Not for the Suns. And so far, not for the Rockets. That's not the dig on Durant that it sounds like. Throughout NBA history, there are very few examples of a team without an incumbent championship superstar winning a ring by way of a hired hand. The 2016 Cavaliers and 2020 Lakers did it with LeBron James, who's the ultimate exception to this rule. He wins everywhere he goes. It's one of the brightest feathers in his GOAT-case cap. 
Other than that, you've got Kawhi Leonard in Toronto, Jalen Brunson in New York, and Kevin Garnett and Ray Allen with the 2008 Celtics as the only examples this century. It just doesn't often happen that a mercenary superstar parachutes into an organization and delivers a title, and certainly not right away. Brunson needed four years and a slew of significant roster moves around him to make it happen with the Knicks. Because Ishbia is right. You generally need an established culture with the right support system, from the role players to the coaches and the front office, in place first. Doing it the other way around is like trying to build a skyscraper on a crap foundation, and we've seen such structures fail over and over. James Harden with, well, every team he's ever gone to after Houston, including Durant's Nets, is the perfect example. All of which is to say, when Ishbia says "bringing in super-talented players like Kevin Durant doesn't necessarily lead to championships," he's just telling the truth. It's pretty convenient, now that we all know how it turned out, that he's saying he never wanted to go the Durant route in the first place, but nonetheless, he's admitting that he messed up in trying to microwave the Suns like an overnight fantasy team. 
You can't do that these days. Especially with the way the aprons are restricting expensive roster building moving forward. There's a reason we don't see teams depleting their rosters -- as the Suns did in offloading the likes of Mikal Bridges, Cam Johnson, Chris Paul, Jae Crowder and Deandre Ayton from their 2021 Finals team -- just to service their superstar fetishes anymore. All Ishbia is saying is he has learned from his own mistakes how important roster depth, coaching and culture are to a championship pursuit, and that even an all-time talent like Durant isn't enough to overcome the absence of those organizational elements. Does Durant have a point, too?In this case, not really. He's right that he "stayed on top of his game at 36" and was individually spectacular in his two and a half seasons with the Suns, as he has been for his entire career, but Ishbia never attacked his personal performance. In fact, he never really personally attacked Durant at all, although you can understand the offense a Hall of Famer would take to being painted as a player with less "Suns DNA," which is code for winning DNA, than Brooks and Gillespie. 
But the bottom line is the Suns, with guys like Brooks and Gillespie playing their ass off every single night, were a better team last year without Durant than they were with him the year prior when they won 36 games and missed the playoffs. Frankly, it's almost baffling that Durant could say with a straight face that he brought the culture back to Ishbia and the Suns. In the two and a half seasons before Durant arrived, the Suns were a model franchise that had made the Finals, finished as the West's No. 1 and No. 2 seeds in consecutive seasons, and won nearly 70% of their regular-season games. In the two and a half years with Durant, they lost nearly half their regular-season games, and in the two full seasons they had him, they got swept in the first round and missed the playoffs entirely. That's not to say any of that was Durant's fault, at least in the sense that he was always individually excellent on the court. Reasonable minds can disagree as to the additive power of Durant's particular basketball brand (it's a question of how much he raises the level of those around him), but never his own production. It's just impossible to compete for championships without all your organizational I's dotted and T's crossed. 
That's the lesson Ishbia is saying he has learned. That you can't win by "throwing money" at your problems. It probably applies more to the Bradley Beal disaster than the trade for Durant, but the general point is the same. You have to fix these problems from the inside out, and the simple truth is that Durant has been parachuting in from the outside trying to save dying teams since he left Golden State. Almost nobody succeeds in that mission. Not even one of the 10-15 greatest players to ever live, as many, including myself, believe Durant to be.
